sentences.text: Start with the furnace alone: in one database of recorded HVAC jobs, traditional fuel-fired heating systems averaged $3,000 less than heat pump installations, though a heat pump also does the cooling.
Another analysis put the extra cost of replacing a house's existing heater with a heat pump, rather than with the same kind of heater, at an average of $6,600.

sentences.text: Another study adds a catch: heat pumps designed to carry all of a home's heating are often more expensive to install than an air conditioner plus gas furnace, because bigger heating loads need bigger heat pumps, new wiring and sometimes panel upgrades.

hybrid or dual-fuel systems) are often more expensive to install than an equivalent
air conditioner plus gas furnace in practice. The main reason is that larger heating loads
require larger heat pumps (or electric resistance backup), new wiring, and sometimes

sentences.text: And real installs spread widely: in the first database, a heat pump's price depended most on its size and type, the home's floor area, the efficiency and the climate zone, and ground-source systems cost far more than other types.

excerpt.text:
A total of 642 heat pump installations were recorded in the database, with a median cost of $8,027.
The median normalized costs were $5.44 per ft2 and $3,387 per ton. Installation costs vary
substantially by the type of heat pump installed, as shown in Figure 57. Ground source heat pumps
were the most expensive, at nearly three times the total system cost of other ductless and ducted heat
pump types. Ductless heat pump systems were more expensive than traditional air source heat pumps
(ASHP), though they commonly had much higher heating and cooling efficiency. Regression analysis
showed that the most important variables in determining heat pump cost include the capacity of the
system (tons), the heat pump type (e.g., ductless mini-split vs. single-stage split heat pump), the
home’s floor area (cfa_post), the cooling and heating efficiencies (SEER and HSFP), Climate Zone, the
Program the project participated in (program_participation), and the number of stories (stories_post).
Less important variables included the location of the unit (location), the home vintage (vintage20), etc.

sentences.text: Then there is the electrical work: in a field test of cold-climate heat pump prototypes at 21 sites, 38 percent needed a new panel.
Where electrical upgrades were needed, they alone cost between $3,750 and $8,970 in labour and materials, before the heat pump itself.
That was a small test, and a typical panel upgrade on its own is put at $1,954 in the first database's report, plus the wiring for each new dedicated circuit.

sentences.text: And on May 29, 2026, the Department of Energy changed the rules: the rebate no longer pays to replace gas or other fossil-fuel equipment, only to upgrade existing electric equipment.
North Carolina's energy office, for one, says its program had to make the change by September 1, 2026.

excerpt.doc: North Carolina 2026, Energy Saver program changes
excerpt.text:
On May 29, 2026, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) issued updated program guidance for the Home
Energy Rebates programs, which includes changes that impact Energy Saver North Carolina.

DOE’s updated guidance for HOMES and HEAR (Program Notice 26-1 and Program Notice 26-2) must be
implemented by Sept. 1, 2026. To meet these requirements, multiple program changes will take effect.

Major HEAR Updates

Fuel Switching Projects are NOT allowed: Rebates will no longer be allowed for the replacement of
gas or any other fossil fuel appliances through the HEAR rebates pathway.

Electric-to-Electric Upgrades ARE allowed: HEAR rebates are now permitted to replace existing
electric appliances with more efficient electric equipment
excerpt.highlight: Fuel Switching Projects are NOT allowed

sentences.text: So before you compare quotes, decide what you would otherwise buy: a furnace alone, or a furnace and an air conditioner.
Ask every installer up front whether your panel and service can carry the heat pump, and check your state energy office and your utility for rebates before you sign.
